title: C24104220149
paper_title: 基于多因素分析与深度学习的磁芯损耗建模

strengths: uses interpretable waveform descriptors before classification
compares three classifier families and reports Accuracy/Recall/F1
uses a simple two-feature classification route that is suitable as a baseline
risks: all three classifiers report 1.00 Accuracy/Recall/F1, but the visible text does not define the independent grouping unit of train/test; row-level perfect classification is not evidence for unseen material/frequency/Bm regimes
the manuscript says models are finally trained on the complete training set and evaluated on a test set, while the exact split construction is not reproducible from the printed appendix
PCA is used during feature exploration, but the final classifier appears to use kurtosis and peak factor; the final feature-selection contract should be stated explicitly
label-driven feature screening and hyperparameter selection should be nested inside each CV fold; the visible paper does not establish that this was done before the reported perfect metrics

strengths: compares several explicit correction hypotheses and several optimizers
reports R2/RMSE/MAPE rather than only fitted parameters
printed appendix contains an actual dynamic-parameter PSO class with inertia/cognitive/social schedules
risks: the abstract says dynamic PSO improves R2 over constant-parameter PSO by 0.041, but the visible uncorrected comparison table reports both as 0.9448; this claim is not supported by that table
dynamic PSO is not uniformly best: for the cubic correction least squares has higher R2/lower RMSE, while dynamic PSO has lower MAPE; optimizer ranking is metric-dependent
the main gain 0.9955-0.9448=0.0507 is attributable to temperature correction plus fitting, not evidence that dynamic PSO alone provides that gain
calibration and model comparison are on the same temperature support; unseen-temperature/generalization evidence is not visible

strengths: visualizes single-factor and crossed-factor distributions before selecting a low-loss condition
risks: pairwise crossed means/boxplots are called synergistic effects, but no explicit interaction term, factorial model, contrast or interaction effect size is estimated; co-varying group means do not establish synergy
frequency and Bm are not adjusted, so raw means can be confounded by operating-condition distributions
the three-factor plot reuses the same attachment data to confirm the condition inferred from the same data; this is consistency within-sample, not independent validation

route: paper claims 10D engineered vector: Bm max + temperature + frequency + material one-hot + waveform one-hot
claimed feature-weight extraction + CNN + Bi-LSTM regression
strengths: separates validation and test in the prose and includes a perturbation stress test
log-transforming the long-tailed loss target is a reasonable candidate transform if evaluated correctly
risks: printed Program 2 is headed Bi-LSTM but defines only CNNModel/Conv1d and contains no visible nn.LSTM; the named final architecture is not reproduced by the appendix

paper says the final input is 10D, while Program 2 uses input_size=1033; Program 4 exposes a 1033-component schema (1024 flux samples + condition/category features), so the architecture comparison also confounds feature schema
Program 3 traditional CNN uses input_size=10 while Program 2 uses 1033, so the reported superiority cannot be attributed cleanly to the claimed architecture when inputs differ

the manuscript interprets K-S statistic 0.2988 > 0.05 as proof of a long-tail distribution, apparently mixing a test statistic with a p-value/significance threshold; the test does not establish the stated distributional claim
random split and synthetic Gaussian perturbation do not establish cross-material/cross-condition generalization; grouped leave-condition-out tests are still required

route: two objectives: minimize predicted core loss and maximize f*Bm
claimed normalized weighted scalarization with weight a
GA vs PSO for scalarized route
strengths: explicitly recognizes objectives have different units and should be normalized
retains an actual Pareto route instead of relying only on one weighted sum
correctly notes that a final Pareto point requires a preference/selection rule
risks: the text says objectives are normalized, but Eq. 8.3 is written directly in Fs and Fe and no reproducible normalization transform is visible; replaying the raw displayed formula does not match Table 8.2 objective values

the preference weight a is itself optimized as a decision variable. A trade-off weight should normally encode stakeholder preference/sensitivity, not be freely chosen by the same optimizer, otherwise the optimization can change the preference to improve its own score
Table 8.3 contains visible feasibility violations relative to Table 8.1: a MOPSO example has Bm=0.4261>0.3133 and another has f=49910<50000

NSGA-II is declared better than MOPSO mainly because the plotted points look more concentrated; a fair stochastic multiobjective comparison needs matched evaluation budgets/seeds and indicators such as hypervolume, IGD/GD, spread and feasibility rate
no Q5 GA/PSO/NSGA-II/MOPSO implementation is visible in the printed appendix (only Programs 1-4), so the final optimizer comparison is not reproducible from the appendix

Table 8.1/prose and constraint equation contain visible registry drift (e.g. 75 vs 70 in the temperature table/text and an apparent frequency-upper-bound mismatch in the rendered equation), reinforcing the need for one machine-readable domain registry

verified_text_evidence.claim: Q1 waveform features, classifiers and all-1.00 reported classification metrics
Q2 correction families, optimizer comparison and printed dynamic-PSO implementation
Q3 single/pair/triple factor mean/variance based synergy reasoning
Q4 claimed Bi-LSTM/10D route, reported metrics, and printed CNN/1033-feature code mismatch
Q5 scalarization, GA/PSO table, Pareto examples and NSGA-II-vs-MOPSO conclusion

transfer_lessons: A method name in the paper must resolve to the actual architecture in code; a heading saying Bi-LSTM does not substitute for an LSTM layer.
Architecture comparisons must keep the input schema and split fixed; changing 10 engineered features to 1033 raw-plus-context features confounds attribution.
Synergy/interaction claims require an explicit interaction estimand or factorial contrast, not only pairwise crossed means.
Test-statistic values and p-values have different semantics; never compare the wrong quantity with alpha.
Preference weights in scalarization are decision policy parameters, not ordinary optimization variables; analyze sensitivity rather than allowing the optimizer to choose its own preference.
Pareto optimizer claims require feasibility replay and quantitative front-quality indicators under matched budgets/random seeds.
Every reported optimum/front sample must be replayed against the same domain registry used by the optimizer and manuscript tables.
